findings.reason: The protected implementation uses bitwise XOR cancellation across all node values and all child node values to identify the root's value in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space, then locates the corresponding Node object in a second linear pass. The algorithm is concise, optimal, and matches the O(1) space follow-up requirement; no candidate is required.

In any valid tree, every non-root node appears twice (once as a node in the array, once as a child in its parent's children list). XORing all node values and child values cancels every non-root value because x XOR x = 0. The root appears only once (as a node, never as a child), so the final XOR accumulator equals the root's value.
Iterating over N nodes and N-1 total child references twice takes O(N) time. Only constant auxiliary variables are used, giving O(1) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts an arbitrarily ordered list of Node objects, handles single-node trees and deep/wide trees correctly, and returns the exact root Node reference.

The approach accurately details parent cancellation via XOR, proves independence of array permutation and tree topology, and states O(N) time and O(1) space complexity. Alternatives and edge cases cover child-value hash sets, sum cancellation with overflow risks, repeated parent searches, single nodes, non-consecutive values, and random order.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the exact same XOR cancellation loop and second-pass lookup with SHA-256 digests e741dc524e7be044d8cf540fa55142559bd0eab115535358e4bf4fe1ebfce518 and ca6368e1655b090e203990e901de6afa0573c75a656520a0930ecb88f80bb25a.
